title: Don't delay inquests into police shootings
article: Nearly seven months after Keldon McMillan was shot and killed by police and more than eight months after Melvin Bigsky died after being shot by an RCMP officer, there's no word on when public inquiries will be held to establish the details in these cases.

While inquiries into cases involving fatal police shootings are a matter of custom rather than mandated by law in Saskatchewan, there are good reasons for justice officials to convene hearings soon on these two incidents involving aboriginal men.

At a time when the entire country is looking askance at this province over highly publicized allegations of racism involving police dealings with the Native community, it's imperative for justice to be seen to be done.

Certainly, seven months seem more than adequate to conduct the kind of investigation required for a public inquiry into McMillan's death, especially when all accounts indicate more than 10 police officers were present when the fatal shooting took place.

And surely eight months are enough to establish the facts surrounding the shooting of Bigsky by an RCMP officer, apparently after the man became aggressive to the point of wrestling with the Mountie as he tried to handcuff him and ramming a truck into the police cruiser.

In the wake of a recent case involving two Saskatoon police officers who abandoned a Native man on the city's outskirts on a winter night and coroners' inquests into the deaths of a couple of other aboriginal men after release from police custody, the announcement of yet more inquires into police conduct undoubtedly will generate poor publicity.

However, that's no reason to allow any foot-dragging over a timely inquiry into these two fatal shootings or to schedule the hearings with an eye to downplaying their public impact by spacing them out.

A strong case exists for demanding that Saskatchewan adopt measures that require mandatory inquiries into all fatalities involving use of force by police, not just those involving deaths of persons in custody.

Firmly and publicly establishing the circumstances surrounding the death of persons in such cases can only enhance faith in the justice system and restore public confidence in the police by conveying an irrefutable message of accountability.

Such a system protects good cops who are devastated when they have to resort to fatal force, weeds out bad apples and comforts families who suffer the consequences of a loved one coming to a violent end.
